analysis.one_liner: Adds secret-ballot and re-election hurdles that make it much harder for unions to organize and keep representing workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee in July 2015 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's basic labor law to raise the bar for unions at every step. Union representatives would have to win a secret-ballot majority of all employees in a workplace, not just of those who vote; whenever more than half a bargaining unit's workforce turned over, the union would have to win a new election or lose certification and its contract. No strike could begin without a secret-ballot majority of every affected employee, and unions would need written, annually renewed permission from each worker to spend dues on anything beyond bargaining. It also includes some provisions aimed at individuals: every represented worker gets a vote on contracts and strikes whether or not they belong to the union, union elections could use private electronic ballots, and using force or threats in labor disputes would carry criminal penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing organizing drives would gain the most: elections would take longer to schedule, non-voters would count against union representation, and any union whose workforce turned over could lose certification and its contract outright. Individual workers who want out of a union would gain direct routes to decertify it and to withhold dues from non-bargaining spending.

how_it_helps.text: Elections would count all employees in the unit rather than only those voting, so workers who stay home count as votes against union representation.

Whenever more than 50% of a bargaining unit's workforce turns over, expands, or merges, the union must win a new secret paper-ballot election or lose certification, and its existing contract obligations terminate.

No strike could start without the consent of a majority of all affected employees in a secret ballot run by a neutral private organization chosen jointly by the employer and union, and workers must first get a vote on the employer's final contract offer; the union bears the election cost.
Union dues could not fund any purpose beyond collective bargaining without a worker's written authorization, which expires after one year with no automatic renewal.

Every election petition would require a hearing before a qualified hearing officer and resolution of all pre-election issues before any election could be held, with the National Labor Relations Board ruling on every issue before certifying results.

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose members, dues, and bargaining leverage, and could lose certification entirely after ordinary workforce turnover. Workers who rely on collective bargaining would face weaker representation, longer and harder organizing drives, and strikes that are much harder to call.

drawbacks.text: The re-election trigger tied to 50% workforce turnover would force repeated decertification votes in most unionized workplaces over time, since turnover of that size is common, and a lost vote ends the union contract.
Requiring a majority of all employees in the unit rather than of those voting makes certification far harder to win, effectively treating non-participation as opposition.

Mandatory hearings, 14-day notice periods, and resolution of every pre- and post-election issue before certification would stretch out the election process, giving employers more time to campaign against unionization before workers vote.

Requiring employers to hand over a voter list with only names and home addresses, rather than the contact information workers can otherwise be given, limits unions' ability to reach workers during campaigns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some provisions offer real individual protections: written annual consent before dues fund politics, private electronic ballots in union elections, a same vote for nonmembers on contracts and strikes, and criminal penalties for violence or extortion in labor disputes. But the core election, re-election, and strike rules would likely shrink union coverage substantially, and lower union density generally means weaker pay and conditions for the workers involved. A bill titled for employee rights whose dominant measurable effect is shifting bargaining power to employers carries a serious cost that its individual protections do not offset.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on July 28, 2015, joined as original cosponsors by 17 Senate Republicans including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, Lamar Alexander, Ted Cruz, and John McCain.
In total, 32 senators cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it the same day to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017, and no floor vote ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and the workers who rely on them kept the existing election, decertification, and strike rules, because the bill never advanced. Employer groups hoping for the new leverage gained nothing, and workers who wanted easier decertification or dues opt-outs did not get them either.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Employee Rights Act and recruited 17 original Republican cosponsors, including the Senate Majority Leader.

for.name: 32 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral as committee chair and scheduled no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill; he was also one of its original cosponsors.

against.name: Organized labor
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Employee Rights Act as a package that would weaken union representation and bargaining power.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 senators backing the bill were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; because the bill never reached a vote, no roll call shows where the full chamber stood.

industries.note: The all-employee election standard, mandatory re-election after 50% turnover, supermajority strike votes, and dues restrictions would cut union membership, dues revenue, and bargaining leverage. Union survival is tied to workers' collective bargaining power, so in this bill the unions' interest runs alongside union-reliant workers' interest.

industries.industry: Employers, especially companies facing organizing drives or with unionized workforces
industries.note: Slower election timelines, a higher election threshold, easier decertification that terminates contracts, and near-impossible-to-call strikes give employers more leverage to stay union-free or shed union obligations. That gain comes directly at the expense of workers' bargaining power.
